extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in 18th-century English theatrical and fair history
extracted.subtask_description: A historical account and description of theatrical booths, menageries, entertainments, and showmanship at London fairs (principally Bartholomew and Southwark) in the late 17th–early 18th centuries. Covers types of attractions, advertising practices, management, performers, and public reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle (machines, singing, dancing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows advertised as presenting 'the best machines, singing and dancing ever yet in the fair' and productions containing moving machines, fountains, angels, and tableaux (e.g., Noah's flood, machines descending from above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular stagecraft and mechanical devices were central to attracting crowds; bills emphasized elaborate machines and visual novelty (e.g., 'several fountains playing water', 'machines descending from above', 'a multitude of angels').

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of popular dramatic incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring incidents in fair dramas—'the troubles of the lovers, the comical adventures of a man-servant, and the encounter with witches'—appear repeatedly, with variations, under different titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences expected familiar comic motifs; successful drolls recycled and varied established incident types to satisfy fairgoers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and mixture of attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairs contained a wide range of entertainments: booths of jugglers, fencers, boxers, mountebanks, swings, round-abouts, sausage stalls, gambling tables, puppet shows, tight-ropes, tumblers, raree-shows, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful fair presentation sat within a diverse program of amusements; offerings were complementary and competed for attention in a crowded environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and exoticism (rarities/menageries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibitions marketed 'a collection of strange and wonderful creatures' and 'the greatest Rarities that ever was shewn alive'—exotic animals and monstrous curiosities (cassowary, peccary, jackal, satyr-like monkey, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of exotic or monstrous rarities were prime draws; showmen often exaggerated. The presence of unusual animals or 'new' specimens boosted attendance, though authenticity could be dubious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and bill detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills described scenes, attractions, performers, times, and claims of past patronage (e.g., 'to be seen from nine o'clock in the Morning, till 10 at Night', 'have danced before Queen Anne and most of the nobility').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid, exhaustive bills that promised spectacle, listed acts, gave hours, and invoked prestige (royal/noble patronage) were used to entice audiences and convey worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement for gentry/quality (accessibility and comfort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some advertisements promised 'a commodious passage for the quality and coaches' and 'care will be taken that there shall be lights, and people to conduct them to their places.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensuring comfort, easy access, and discrete accommodation for wealthier patrons was a tactic to attract the 'gentry and quality' and to elevate a fair show’s social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger/skill feats and novelty performance types
rubrics_metrics.description: Tight-rope dancing, ladder-dances, dancing with swords, vaulting, 'strong woman' feats, and other hazardous or highly-skilled displays (e.g., a child performing naked-sword dance) featured prominently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feats combining perceived danger and virtuosity were popular attractions; reviving or showcasing rare skills drew crowds and press notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical illusion and moving figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations with moving figures and scenes (painted flat surfaces with cut-out figures set in motion, possibly by clockwork) were used to create spectacular tableaux (e.g., 'divinities of Olympus ascending and descending to the sound of music').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanized motion and illusionary stagecraft allowed fair booths to rival formal operas and theatres in spectacle despite limited space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained animal performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal acts were advertised with specific tricks (a horse 'fetches and carries', seeks hidden objects, 'will also tell the number of spots on a card, and leap through a hoop').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-trained animals performing humanlike or trick behaviors were notable draws and were often highlighted in promotional copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility vs. hyperbole (skepticism toward claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Showmen's claims were often grandiose ('The Wonders of England' pamphlet was a mere 'catch-penny'); advertisements painted monsters not necessarily present 'like the showmen's painted cloths in the fair, pictures monsters not visible within.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences and later commentators are warned to be skeptical of exhibitors' hyperbolic claims; promotional rhetoric frequently overstated content or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular contemporary material and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair adaptations drew on popular operas and dramas (e.g., Beggar's Opera adaptations, Siege of Troy, Wat Tyler) and often trimmed or altered works for fair audiences ('reduced it from five acts to three, striking out four or five of the dramatis personae').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation and condensation of known works into shorter, more comic or spectacular drolls suited fair audiences' tastes and attention spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and talent scouting function of fairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers used fair booths to discover and recruit talent from strolling companies and provincial theatres; notable performers were 'found and transferred to their own boards'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booths functioned as a labor market for theatre managers—successful fair performances could lead to engagements at major metropolitan theatres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic incentives and scheduling (theatres vs. fairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatres sometimes closed during fairs because actors could obtain larger salaries in booths and fairs drew all classes away from theatres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic considerations shaped scheduling and participation; fairs could be more remunerative and thus drew established actors to set up booths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection within the fair
rubrics_metrics.description: Location choices are named (opposite the Crown Tavern, in George Yard, between the hospital gate and the Crown Tavern), implying desirable positions within Smithfield or other fair precincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prime sites (central positions, near gates or taverns) mattered for visibility and audience flow; managers contended for favourable pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management/partnership and ownership practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Booths were often set up by combinations of proprietors, actors, and printers (e.g., Lee the theatrical printer taking a booth; partnerships like Lee and Harper, Fielding and Reynolds), with profits and reputation at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful booth operation relied on managerial partnerships, pooling talent and resources; ownership afforded potential substantial income but also legal/social risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public order and moral/legal risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to exclude 'persons of immoral character' led to riots; arrests of performers for vagrancy occurred, and conflicts with authorities (presentations as a nuisance) could threaten fairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers needed to manage crowds and relations with authorities; moral panics, policing actions, or riots could severely disrupt fairs and lead to suppression attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige via royal/noble patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that performers or animals 'had the Honour to be show'd before Queen Anne, Prince George, and most of the Nobility' were used to confer prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoking royal or noble patronage in advertising lent legitimacy and attracted audiences seeking endorsed entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating hours and attendant services
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows specified operating times ('to be seen from nine o'clock in the Morning, till 10 at Night') and promised 'true Attendance' during stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear stated hours and promises of attendant service reassured visitors and framed expectations for the experience.
